Remarks: Out looking for an endangered orchid, and came across this little critter
Comment: Ross: I am sure this is a Spicebush Swallowtail caterpillar, as per one of the photos on page 81 of the Caterpillars of Eastern North America (Wagner). During the first 3 instars, the Spicebush caterpillar normally resembles a bird dropping according to that reference. The black eyespots and the white pattern of this individual seems to fit an immature Spicebush. I have seen larvae of Giants, which do not look quite like this in my experience. It was found on a Spicebush also and was well inside a hardwood forest type where Spicebush is abundant. Host plants for Giant Swallowtail larvae include hoptree and prickly ash, neither of which occur with several hundred metres of where this caterpillar was found.

This one is a conundrum. I took this photo in our back yard, much of which is natural vegetation or vegetable garden, and Campbell Park is on two sides of us. My wife alerted me to a skipper in the yard, resting on chives. I got this one photo before it leapt up I never saw it again in spite of looking for a couple of hours. I felt it was not a skipper I had seen before and in looking through both Glassberg and the ROM guide, I concluded it may be a Zabulon. I sent it to several others who are more knowledgeable than I am, including Paul Pratt, Donald Sutherland, Mike Burrell, Colin Jones, Blake Mann and Alan Wormington. I know skippers can be challenging, especially if only a single photo is available which does not show all the critical characters. However there is no consensus. Without naming who voted which way, I have had three votes for Zabulon, three for Peck's and one for Sachem! So more input is needed, or maybe leave it as skipper sp.

Comment: A bit of a surprise, as I have seen very few of this species locally. Large, more like Cloudless than Clouded Sulfur, with falcate forewings obvious when resting with folded wings a few feet away. Dorsal color yellow; through binoculars, at rest, ventral side tinged greenish with some pinkish veins. Forewing with much black at apex (much more than Clouded or Orange), and "dog face" showing through clearly in backlit ventral view. Very "flighty," landing frequently but never for more than 3-4 seconds at a time, which meant that I was unable to obtain a photograph.

Comment: Kory Renaud found 1 adult on June 13 at this location and put the word out. Knowing that it can be colonial three of us looked more closely at the meadow from the trail and saw presumably the same individual that Kory saw yesterday in pretty much the same area. We moved on a found another spot that had at least 4 other adults. We scanned the meadow from our slightly higher elevation and on two occasions in a 10 minute or so period saw two instances of one Baltimore chasing another before disappearing into deeper vegetation. The two chases were separated by about 30 metres so we felt that the chases involved 4 individuals. We felt that there could be many more individuals in this meadow but we decided not to venture into the taller grasses and herbs due to the high number of ticks this year.
